- The account list is a real list with its own regex-wired search, per-account sign-out, set-active
  and token-refresh actions, and an add-account path running the same sign-in flow as the first.
- Offer **copy-and-push as an alternative to forking**. Forking is provider-specific and unsupported
  on some instances; an app that only forks cannot publish there. Do not present a fork button
  guaranteed to fail — offer the route that works and say why. Report which route was taken, and
  never silently substitute one for the other.

## Export everything, in every format

- **Every record, view, list, log, document, setting and generated artifact is exportable.** If a
  surface can show it, the user can take it away. "You can copy it from the screen" is not an export.
- Offer every format that can faithfully represent the data — JSON, JSONL, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, TSV,
  Markdown, HTML, SQL, and language-source forms where they make sense. Pick per datum rather than
  per app, and never offer a format that would silently drop a field. Where a format cannot carry
  something, say what will be lost *before* the export runs.
- Exports are complete and re-importable where the shape allows a round trip. State the encoding,
  line endings, and schema or version so the file is readable by something other than the app that
  wrote it.
- **Archives expose everything the format actually offers** rather than a hard-coded default:
  compression methods, levels from store through ultra, dictionary and block sizes, solid mode,
  multi-threading, split volumes, and both content encryption and **encrypted headers** so filenames
  are hidden too. Explain what each costs in time and memory, and never present an encrypted archive
  as protected while leaving its filenames in the clear.
- Archive exports name what is inside, keep paths relative so extraction cannot escape its directory,
  and never place a secret in an archive the surrounding flow has not clearly marked as sensitive.
- **Every export lands in an editor**: one action from the export or its originating record opens the
  file or folder in the user's editor, detecting an existing install and offering the download when
  none is found rather than failing silently. Opening a folder opens it as a workspace root.

## Bulk actions everywhere

- **Every list, table, grid and collection supports bulk actions.** Selecting one item and repeating
  an action forty times is the app failing to do its job. Provide multi-select with click,
  shift-click ranges and a keyboard equivalent, a select-all that states plainly whether it means
  *this page* or *every match*, and an inverse selection.
- **This is not exempt for the notification centre or any history panel — they are lists too, and
  "it's just a log" is not an excuse.** Same multi-select, same honestly-scoped select-all, bulk
  dismiss, bulk delete behind the destructive-action gate, and a bulk export honouring the active
  filter rather than dumping the entire unfiltered log.
- Offer the whole set of actions in bulk, not a token subset: delete, export, move, copy, duplicate,
  rename by pattern, tag, enable/disable, retry, and whatever else the surface offers singly. Bulk
  search and filter compose with selection, and the regex builder applies here as everywhere.
- **Say what will happen before it happens**: the exact count and a reviewable preview, distinguishing
  "42 selected" from "42 will change" when some are skipped. Never let a bulk action silently skip
  items — report what was excluded and why.
- Bulk actions are undoable through the same local version history, or explain plainly why one
  cannot be. Long-running ones report progress, remain cancellable, and state partial results
  honestly rather than claiming a whole batch succeeded.

## Local version control

- Every app that owns user documents or projects provides a local, version-controlled history:
  complete per-document snapshots in an isolated repository beside the app's own data directory —
  **never a repository inside the user's own folder** — with a first-class history panel to browse,
  diff, restore and label revisions. Keep it local unless the user explicitly opts in, and provide
  retention, pruning and export controls.
- **This is not limited to documents. Every app snapshots every user-managed record it owns** —
  accounts, credentials, connected services, generators, rules and **settings** — so any creation,
  edit or deletion can be undone. An app that version-controls its documents but silently loses an
  account the user deleted by mistake has satisfied the letter of the rule and none of its point.
  Settings belong in the same snapshot as the records they configure: restoring an account without
  the configuration it ran under is a subtly wrong state, and worse than offering no undo at all.
- **Restoring is itself recorded as a new revision, never a rewrite**, so an undo can be undone, and
  that undo undone in turn. A destructive "restore" that discards the branch it replaced is the one
  failure mode that makes a history panel unsafe to use.
- Snapshots preserve whatever encryption the live data uses, so history is never more sensitive than
  the store it mirrors. **Bind any authenticated-encryption associated data to a stable identifier
  that survives delete and restore**, not to an autoincrement row id: a restored row receives a fresh
  id, the binding stops matching, and the data becomes permanently undecryptable while failing in a
  way that looks exactly like corruption.
- The panel is filterable, with at minimum a **date picker** and a **filter by action**. Filtering by
  action means the real actions derived from the history itself — created, updated, deleted, restored,
  undone, imported, settings changed — not a hard-coded list that drifts. Show the count beside each,
  allow more than one at once, and compose the action filter with the date range and text search. Its
  search bar carries the full regex builder, and the empty result is an honest no-match message.
- Label each revision with what changed rather than that something did. An unchanged state records
  nothing. A history write that fails must never fail the operation the user actually asked for.

## Blank-slate editors offer presets

An editor that opens to nothing offers presets and a first-class path to start from the
application's own defaults, rather than handing the user an empty canvas and calling that a feature.
Presets derive strictly from the real defaults and templates — never an invented value dressed up as
a starting point — so a preset and the "reset to defaults" path can never disagree.

Each preset states exactly what it creates and sets, so choosing one is an informed action rather
than a guess about what just happened. The result is fully editable and undoable through the same
local version history as any other change.

## Changelog viewer

- Every app ships an in-app changelog viewer covering **every** released version, reachable from a
  discoverable place. Each entry carries version, release date and categorized changes. A link to
  release notes on a website does not satisfy this.
- Provide a **date filter** with an advanced calendar picker — month and year jump, range selection,
  presets — that also accepts **typed dates**, parsing the locale format and plain ISO. Invalid or
  partial input is reported inline without discarding what the user typed.
- Provide a **search over changelog text** wired to the full regex builder, with plain text the
  default. Search and date filter compose rather than override one another, and the empty result is
  an honest no-match message.
- Support **export and copy** honouring the active filter and search, stating the exported range.
- The viewer obeys the language modes and funny-level sliders, which style every entry including
  security fixes and breaking changes — while version numbers, dates and what actually changed stay
  exact.
- Changelog content is factual: never invent entries, dates or fixes. A version with no recorded
  changes says so.
- **Every entry links to the commit that made the change.** An entry saying what changed but not
  where is unverifiable. Carry the full commit identifier, render it as a short clickable reference,
  and resolve it against the project's own forge. A wrong identifier is worse than none — validate
  that every referenced commit exists before shipping, and fail the build rather than emitting a
  dead link.
- **The changelog is brought current in every project-changing task**, not at release time. A viewer
  documenting the past while misleading about the present is worse than none; catch it up from the
  real commit history rather than from memory.

## Universal file converter

Every app and page ships a real local file-converter surface accepting a user-selected source
through a guided picker with an honest empty state, detecting type from **bounded byte inspection
rather than extension**, and presenting compatible choices from a documented adapter registry as a
categorized, searchable catalogue — never one flat target dropdown. Each category has its own
keyboard-accessible search and adjacent anchored regex builder, and lists every format supplied by
an installed verified adapter **and every known unavailable format as visible disabled content with
the exact missing dependency**. It never hides a capability gap.

**Enabled adapters are bundled, proven, explicit, bounded and fail closed.** A format is available
only when every dependency is bundled inside the installed application and works offline. Path
discovery, a developer-machine tool, a network service or an unbundled optional dependency must never
make a format appear enabled. Run decoders in a least-privileged isolated process with allowlisted
arguments, no ambient network, and bounded bytes, counts, CPU time, memory, recursion depth,
temporary storage and cancellation. Validate produced output by type, signature, parse or round-trip
before offering it. An unknown, malformed, encrypted or limit-exceeding source stays untouched and
reports the exact boundary; never write guessed, truncated, mislabeled or corrupt output.

**Document tooling is complete and verified**: inspect, split, merge, extract, reorder, rotate and
metadata operations, with their exact capability limits stated before execution. Every write is
atomic and never exposes a partial destination. **Post-write reopening validates the resulting page
order, count, rotation and metadata against the request** before reporting success; any mismatch
removes the temporary output and reports the exact failure without leaking a source path, secret,
document content or network detail.

**Conversion choices stay informed and reversible.** Before a lossy or metadata-changing conversion,
disclose exactly what can change or be omitted — transparency, layers, colour profile, animation,
fonts, metadata, line endings, character encoding, fields, precision — and require an explicit
action. Preserve the source unchanged, write output atomically to an approved destination, avoid
overwriting without the confirmation gate, and give a per-file batch result distinguishing converted,
skipped, cancelled and failed.

**The queue has no artificial cap and never loads every path or byte into memory.** Accept an
unlimited-length queue through paged discovery and a persistent resumable record, then process
bounded-concurrency chunks with constant-memory backpressure. Per-file size and safety bounds remain
mandatory. Provide pause, resume and cancel; keep per-file progress and outcomes; preflight
destination capacity; recover after a crash or restart; and resume only files whose durable state and
validation permit it.

## Local model-runtime suite manager

Every app and page ships a complete local model-runtime suite manager using only the runtime's
documented local HTTP API for health, version, installed and running models, tags, pulls, deletes,
copies, generation, chat and capability metadata. It never calls an unofficial proxy, embeds a cloud
service, or claims the runtime can launch arbitrary programs.

**Every operation is fully guided.** Populate model, tag, variant, quantization, context, parameter,
destination and harness choices from verified real data and registered profiles; recommend a safe
default with its reason while retaining a validated advanced path; and explain every model family and
variant, capability, size and storage implication before selection. Never present a blank or
freeform-only field where a safe picker can supply the value, and never send the user to search the
web to discover the next step. Every disabled control names its exact unmet condition and the exact
next in-app action. Missing, stopped, unhealthy or offline states provide bundled offline
documentation and an in-app troubleshooter with detected status, platform-appropriate guidance,
verification and a return path to the interrupted action.

**The catalogue is exhaustive at each verified refresh, never curated.** Enumerate every model and
published variant through the official sources, following all pagination, and record the source
revision, refresh timestamp, page count and completeness verdict. Combine it with locally installed
tags without hiding either set; show staleness and a refresh action; and while offline show only the
last verified catalogue plus current installed state, never guessed entries.

**Hardware fit is conservative evidence, not a promise.** Detect system memory, GPU, usable video
memory, driver support, free disk and architecture, combine with exact model size, parameter count,
quantization and declared context window, and give every variant one of *runs well*, *runs with
limits*, *unlikely* or *unknown* — exposing the evidence and assumptions, timestamped, recomputed
when anything changes. Never infer capability from a model name or treat missing metadata as zero.

**The cart means batch pull only and never money.** There is no price, purchase, checkout, account,
payment or subscription. Before starting, show each exact tag, download size, conservative additional
disk requirement, free space, transfer disclosure and fit verdict. Process with bounded parallelism,
durable per-item state, byte-accurate progress, cancellation, retry and safe resume, with honest
partial outcomes. A failed item never turns the batch green or deletes a valid installed model.

**Harness launch is allowlisted orchestration by the app, never a runtime capability.** Ship prebuilt
profiles and allow registration only through semantic pickers and allowlisted executable, argument,
working-directory and environment schemas. **Never accept an arbitrary shell command, script text,
command concatenation or unvalidated environment expansion.** Before launch, run a visible preflight
naming the model, executable, arguments, working directory, environment keys with secrets redacted,
required ports and exact blockers. Snapshot the profile and configuration before every mutation,
offer one-click restore, and roll back automatically when launch or health verification fails.
Secrets stay in the operating-system credential vault and never enter snapshots, arguments, logs,
history, exports, captures or source.

## Build and dependency scripts at every repository root

**Every repository carries a one-click build script at its root** that takes a checkout with nothing
installed and produces a built, runnable program without the user knowing anything about the
toolchain.

- **Assume a fresh machine, and be touchless.** No runtime, no package manager, no SDK, no build
  tools, no compiler. The script obtains every one of them itself, without a prompt, without a manual
  download, and without a sentence beginning "Install X and run this again". Prefer the platform
  package manager for a user-scoped install, and fall back to a portable extract into a per-user
  toolchain directory.
  - **Refresh the current process's PATH after an install rather than assuming it.** A package
    manager writes PATH for *future* shells, so the very next command in the same script still cannot
    find what was just installed — a mistake that reads as "the install failed" when it succeeded.
  - The only acceptable stopping point is a genuinely unobtainable dependency, reported with the
    exact routes tried.
- It installs everything itself, checking first and installing only what is missing, from canonical
  upstreams, into per-project or user-scoped locations. It never requires administrator rights when a
  user-scoped path exists, never mutates an unrelated global toolchain, and never asks the user to
  install something by hand.
- It builds the real artifact through the project's own supported packaging path — the same one CI
  uses.
- **Then it asks whether to run it**, last rather than first, so a failed build never offers to launch
  nothing.
- It has a **silent mode** installing and building with no prompt, no interactive pause and no window,
  exiting non-zero on the first real failure so a caller can branch on it.
- **It reports honestly** per phase: what it found installed, what it installed and where, how long it
  took. A failure names the exact missing dependency, version constraint, source tried and blocking
  error — never a bare "build failed".
- **It is idempotent and safe to re-run**, reusing caches and leaving nothing half-written.
- It never installs secrets, credentials or a signing certificate, and never weakens the machine's
  persistent execution policy.

**A second script beside it produces the installer** — the same artifact CI publishes, through the
same packaging path, at the same version, so a locally built installer and a released one are the
same thing rather than two things that resemble each other. Same contract: self-installing
dependencies, silent mode, honest per-phase reporting, idempotence, no signing. It **verifies what it
built** — the file exists, is the expected size and shape, came from the intended commit — and reports
the artifact path and its hash. It never publishes, tags, pushes or creates a release: building an
installer and shipping it are different actions with different authority.

**Agents ship every manual release through these scripts, never around them.** Not because it is
tidier, but because a script that only ever runs on a warm developer machine is a script nobody has
proven works, and the first time it is genuinely needed is the worst time to find out. If a script
fails during a manual release, **the fix is to the script**, in a commit, before the release goes
out; working around it once is how it stays broken for the next person.

**A dependency fetcher sits beside them**, obtaining every dependency from canonical upstreams into
per-project or user-scoped locations. It **pins an exact version and verifies a recorded digest for
every binary it places on disk** — an unverified downloaded binary is a supply-chain hole, and it is
the one part that cannot be fixed later by reading the code. It keeps a committed manifest of those
versions and digests so a human can audit what a build puts on their machine without running it.
Idempotent, silent-capable, honest per phase. Fetched dependencies are never committed. The build
script calls it rather than duplicating it, so the two cannot drift.

## Every app bundles its dependencies

**Every user-facing app ships every dependency it needs inside its own installer.** Not a link, not
a prompt, not a page of instructions, not a first-run wizard sending someone to a vendor's download
page. A person who installs the app has installed everything it needs, and it works with the network
unplugged.

- **"Install X and try again" is a defect, in any wording.** So is a button opening a browser at a
  runtime, SDK, CLI or redistributable.
- **Bundle by preference, obtain automatically as the fallback, link never.** Where a licence forbids
  redistribution, the app obtains the dependency itself — verified, pinned, unattended, with real
  progress where the person started it.
- **Prefer the portable distribution** where one exists, and never require administrator rights for a
  dependency with a user-scoped form.
- A dependency the app can fall back to on the machine still resolves bundled-first, and the surface
  says which is in use. Somebody debugging a version mismatch cannot do it otherwise.
- **Say the size honestly** in the release notes rather than letting a download size quietly triple.

**Not everything a link points at is a dependency.** An optional integration target the person
chooses — their editor, browser, terminal, a server they run elsewhere — is not bundled. The test is
whether the app is *complete without it*. For those, a link is legitimate, but the copy must never
read as a prerequisite the person failed to satisfy: say the app is fully functional without it, and
detect what is already installed before concluding there is none. Name this distinction in the
project's documentation so a later agent does not "fix" a correct optional link, or excuse a real
dependency as an optional one.

### A bundled dependency the app cannot find is worse than no bundling at all

This failure is invisible from both ends and has happened: a packaging configuration shipped an
engine inside the installer, and the application never looked there — the resources root was not
exposed on its process bridge at all. A freshly installed build carried a bundled engine it could not
see, reported it as missing, and offered a download link for the very file inside its own
installation directory. Nothing failed: packaging succeeded, the installer was correct, the release
verified, and the only symptom was an app telling people to fetch something they already had.

- **Adding a file to the packaging config is half a change.** The other half is the code that
  resolves it, and the two land in the same commit or the bundle is dead on arrival.
- **A "not found" state must enumerate every location it searched**, so a dead bundle shows up as a
  path nobody looked in rather than a missing file.
- **Prove it from the built artifact, not the config.** Install the package and confirm the app
  resolves the bundled tool and reports its origin. A green packaging log proves a file was copied,
  never that anything can find it.
- The same shape appears one layer up, in the pipeline: a pre-script hook that only fires for the
  script it is named after will never run if CI invokes the underlying tools directly, so every
  release ships a configuration claiming to bundle a runtime it never fetched. **Call the named
  script from CI rather than hand-copying its steps**, and **assert against the packaged output** —
  a plausible artifact size floor, with the arithmetic written down, is the cheapest second signal.

### A comment asserting a safety property nobody verified is worse than no comment

A packaging config carried a comment stating it "fails loudly on a missing source directory".
Everyone who read it believed a safety net existed. It did not — the underlying tool logs a warning
and returns early, and packaging exits successfully.

- **A comment asserting a tool's behaviour is a claim, and claims get verified or deleted.** If it
  says "this fails loudly", "this is atomic", "this validates", "this cannot happen" — read the
  tool's source or write the failing case and watch it, then record which you did.
- **The direction of the error is what makes it expensive.** A comment understating a guarantee costs
  a little redundant caution. One that *invents* a guarantee removes the check that would have caught
  the bug, and does so specifically for the careful reader who took it at its word.
- When you disprove one, **fix the comment in the same commit** as the real guard.

## Write down what worked, not just what shipped

When something takes more than one attempt to get right, **the working method is a deliverable**. The
next agent starts from zero and will otherwise burn the same attempts in the same order.

- **Record the method, not the anecdote.** "The device flow works, driven directly, because the CLI
  hides its prompt without a terminal" is reusable. "Auth was fiddly" is not.
- **Record the dead ends too, and say they are dead.** A failed approach that looks obviously correct
  is worth more than the successful one, because that is the one that will be tried again.
- **Prefer the shape over the transcript.** A short sketch of the calls, flags or ordering that
  matters travels; a pasted session does not.
- **Write it while it is fresh**, in the same task. The detail that makes the difference is exactly
  the detail that is gone by the next session.
- The same applies to a platform's refusals: an assumption a runner, filesystem or shell cannot
  satisfy is worth recording once so nobody rediscovers it as a red build.

This is not a request for a diary. If a task ran clean, there is nothing to add.

### Recurring traps worth knowing

The maintainer's canonical instructions carry a long catalogue of specific, hard-won debugging
lessons. The generalizable ones:

- **A full-suite run under heavy machine contention manufactures its own failures.** A test that
  fails at exactly the configured timeout timed out; it did not assert anything false. Two cheap
  discriminators settle it: does the failing file reference the changed subsystem at all, and is the
  reported duration sitting on the ceiling? Then re-run that one file alone. **Never raise the
  timeout to make it green** — that hides the next real hang.
- **Capture the runner's exit code inside the log.** A wrapper shaped `(cmd > log 2>&1; echo EXIT=$?;
  tail log)` returns *tail's* status, so a suite that exited non-zero is announced as success.
- **A lazy any-character run in a source-scanning guard swallows whole files.** It matches newlines,
  and "lazy" does not mean "stop at the end of this line or statement", so the pattern reaches past
  the construct it was written for. Bridge tokens on one line or not at all; count delimiters for
  nested structures; a negative assertion with an over-reaching pattern fails on code that is
  correct, which is more confusing than a false pass.
- **Parsing a stylesheet with a regular expression finds less than it reports**: it skips rules
  nested inside at-blocks, and comments become part of the selector. Strip comments, then scan with a
  depth counter.
- **Two ways a guard passes while the thing it guards is gone**: a descendant rule satisfying an
  existence check, and a renamed symbol still containing the original name as a substring. Match the
  selector itself; assert the call including its delimiter.
- **A guard that shares its subject's implementation agrees with its bugs.** A completeness check
  must re-walk the tree with its own code rather than calling the generator's discovery function,
  precisely so it can detect that generator dropping a file.
- **Guard tests catch a thing done wrongly and never a thing not done at all.** A file with no search
  bar passes a rule about search bars carrying builders. Every such rule wants an inverted assertion
  beside it — a **hand-written** list of the surfaces that must have the thing, because a pattern
  guessing which files are settings surfaces stops matching the day somebody renames one.
- **A guard nobody has watched fail proves nothing.** After writing one, break the thing it guards,
  confirm it goes red, then restore.
- **A token or value declared twice is decided by ordering, not by the file you opened.** Editing the
  losing declaration is a silent no-op: the edit is syntactically perfect, tests pass, the build
  succeeds, and the only symptom is that nothing changed — indistinguishable from "the fix was
  unnecessary" unless somebody looks. Find every declaration, check import order, and assert they
  agree.
- **Measure the built app; a stylesheet cannot tell you which rule won.** The same selector written
  twice in one file means the later block silently overrides the earlier one. Add a measurement step
  to the capture harness rather than writing throwaway probe scripts.
- **"The value is stored" and "the class is applied" are not evidence that anything renders.** A
  setting can have a control, write its attribute, persist, pass every test — and change nothing
  visible, because no code reads the property it sets. Follow the property to something that consumes
  it.
- **A component test sees the fallback; the running application sees the catalogue.** A translation
  call has two possible answers, and a unit test only exercises one. Namespace new copy keys and look
  at the built, running application after adding user-visible text.
- **A test that injects the dependency proves the screen and nothing about the wiring.** A UI surface
  tested with an injected host passes whether or not the real bridge exposes the shape it expects.
  Budget a smoke run against the real artifact after wiring any bridge, IPC surface or plugin
  boundary.
- **Thorough tests of a module's pure half say nothing about the half that shells out.** A module with
  a pure decision half and a subprocess half attracts tests to the pure half, because that half is
  easy and satisfying to test well — while the part carrying the feature has never run. Any module
  that spawns a process, opens a socket or writes a file needs at least one test that actually does
  that, asserting through an independent channel. **The tell is a feature whose tests are unusually
  elegant.**
- **A count assertion is usually an assertion about the size of the codebase.** Pinning "exactly one
  match" or "exactly N cards" quietly also says nothing else may ever exist. Retarget to the property
  meant — but note that occasionally such a test is right and has found a genuine duplicate.
- **A subtest count is not a failure count.** One loop over historical data can contribute hundreds of
  failures from a single test function.
- **A fixture captured on one platform makes the test assert the platform it runs on.** Compare with
  line endings normalized and give the platform rule an assertion that states it.
- **A page can be served by more than one compiled entry point** — per theme, per locale, per platform
  — so appending an import to one of them is a partial change, absent for a whole configuration of
  users while the diff looks correct and the build goes green.
- **The wrong repository can look exactly like the right one.** Resolve the destination repository
  before the first commit, not before the first push, and confirm it by fetching and checking the
  merge base — an empty merge base means unrelated histories and nothing built on one can be merged
  into the other. "I asked and got no answer, so I proceeded" is sound for reversible work and
  unsound for a base commit.
- **A stray dependency directory above the checkout makes local type-checking lie**, resolving types
  from outside the repository so a local check is green on code that cannot compile anywhere else.
- **An editable package install names one checkout, and every other checkout borrows it** — and the
  exposure is directional in the counter-intuitive way: the checkout the install names is the safe
  one; every *other* clone is exposed.
- **Repeatedly destroying and recreating an application object corrupts wrapper types** in some
  toolkits, producing failures deep into a run whose message names a class that is still correct.
- **Restoring a patched attribute by assignment is not a restore when it was inherited** — it creates
  a new class attribute holding the base class's unbound method.
- **A fresh bitmap is uninitialised memory, and a window-print call can report success without
  painting anything.** Pure black in a palette containing no black means those pixels were never
  drawn.
- **Design pixel sizes are not point sizes**, and the difference is about a third — uniformly, which
  reads as "the app is oversized" rather than as a bug.
- **A scaled minimum window size must be clamped to the display it opens on**, or a laptop gets a
  window it physically cannot fit — on that machine only.
- **Many agents over one checkout will clobber work and contaminate every measurement.** Agents stage
  only their own explicit paths and commit promptly; no full-suite verdict is trusted unless the tree
  was quiet for its whole duration.
- **A fixed list of captured states photographs the states somebody thought of; driving the
  application reaches the ones nobody did.** Keep the scripted set as the regression gate and drive
  the app when you want to find something new.
- **A capture harness that records an unreachable surface as a gap instead of failing lets a real
  defect through a green run.** Split the surfaces: ones needing a runtime or account stay soft
  skips; ones needing nothing but the application get an assertion that fails the run.
- **A pool consumed once per release runs out, and running out is usually designed to be non-fatal —
  which means invisible.** Size it against the real cadence and make exhaustion emit a warning.
- **A string a test waits for has two owners.** Renaming the product string alone does not go red; the
  wait silently becomes a no-op and the suite starts failing later, elsewhere. Export the literal once
  and import it at every wait.
- **Write a constraint as a policy, never as an absence.** "There is no local toolchain" gets
  disproven and then ignored; "X is installed and is deliberately not used here, because Y" survives.

## Working discipline

- Prefer reversible, auditable changes and headless verification. Do not overwrite user content,
  credentials or existing agent instructions; use owned files or clearly delimited managed blocks.
- Read repository-local agent instructions and relevant feature documentation before editing. Keep
  changes scoped, run proportionate tests, and report concrete evidence.
- Treat host inventories and service lists as point-in-time routing hints, not authorization to
  mutate those systems. Recheck live state before deployment.
- **After a multi-agent feature workflow lands, run a detailed adversarial bug-hunt pass over its
  changes before the integration commit.** Use more than one finder lens — correctness, security,
  accessibility, whichever the change actually touches — and loop each until it comes back dry.
  Route findings through independent refuters that vote before acceptance, so a single overeager
  finder cannot manufacture work out of nothing, and regression-test every resulting fix.
- When the user pins orchestration to a specific model, pin **every** agent in the pass to it —
  finders, judges, refuters, fixers and capture agents alike, not only the finders.

### A green build on a warm tree is not evidence the build works

Several CI failures share one shape, invisible on the machine you develop on: **the build succeeded
locally because something an earlier attempt left behind was quietly satisfying a prerequisite
nobody had declared.** CI is a cold checkout every time, so it is the only place the omission shows
up — and it shows up as a failure that looks nothing like a missing prerequisite.

- **Naming a late-stage target skips every pass before it.** A packaging target runs the packaging
  pass and only that; earlier builds had left the binaries on disk, so it packed artifacts it played
  no part in producing and exited successfully. On a cold checkout it fails with a missing-file error
  that reads as a packaging defect rather than "nothing ever built this".
- **A dependency installed with default options is a dependency installed incompletely**, and the
  failure arrives much later as a link error naming a file that never existed.
- **Find every requirement at once instead of one CI round at a time.** A build system that declares
  its dependencies declares all of them somewhere greppable; sweeping for them takes one command,
  while discovering them serially costs a round trip each.
- **Whenever you add a requirement to a dependency, that dependency's presence check becomes wrong in
  the same commit.** Grep the whole file for the existing check rather than fixing the one you were
  told about — a half-fix fails identically, much later, with the correct fix sitting visibly in the
  diff doing nothing.
- **Add a post-install assertion separately from the guard.** The guard decides whether to install;
  the assertion decides whether the install worked.
- **Say the warm-tree part out loud when reporting.** A local run that exits 0 on a tree with many
  builds of residue is a real artifact and is *not* evidence the script works from clean. An artifact
  proves the artifact exists, never that the path which produced it is reproducible.

### Two ways a build system picks the wrong thing and never says so

- **A loop that "selects" by iterating to the end selects the last, not the best.** Sorting
  descending and then walking without a break lands on the *oldest* entry. Whenever a sort is
  followed by a loop with no break, ask what the loop is actually selecting.
- **A path separator can silently route a lookup to a directory that exists and is wrong.** Mixed
  separators defeat a prefix comparison, sending a fallback search to a plausibly-named directory
  whose real contents live one level deeper. This is worse than a missing path, because every
  diagnostic looks reasonable: the directory is there, the variable is set, nothing is empty.
- **The rule both share: fix the producer, never the consumer.** Patching the consumer to tolerate a
  bad value masks a real defect, leaves it live for every other caller, and puts a local edit
  somewhere the next update silently reverts.
- **Put the assertion where the value is produced, not where it is used**, and watch it fail on the
  real bad value before trusting it.

## Skill scope and persistence

- These shared instructions apply to **every repository a task touches**, not only the primary one —
  including linked worktrees, submodules, tooling repositories, documentation repositories and any
  secondary repository reached during the same task. A repository is not exempt because the work
  there is only a supporting step.
- Apply them independently at each repository boundary while preserving stricter repository-local
  rules.
- A project-local instruction file may add stricter requirements or narrow scope, but may not
  silently disable a globally applicable rule. If local instructions conflict with these, stop and
  report the conflict rather than guessing.
